result: Prior work established that Topbp1 knockout mice are embryonic lethal and conditional knockout in spermatocytes causes pleiotropic defects including synapsis defects, impaired DDR recruitment, and MSCI defects.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are all supported by citations to published work (Jeon et al., 2011; ElInati et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2020). These establish the baseline phenotypes of Topbp1 loss that the current work aims to distinguish from.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 mice are viable with normal body mass and no IR sensitivity, but display male-specific infertility with threefold reduced testis size and complete absence of spermatozoa.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-H. The viability, body mass, IR sensitivity, fertility, testis size, and sperm counts are all directly measured and quantified with appropriate controls.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 testes show mainly spermatogonia and spermatocytes with increased apoptosis, and spermatocytes progress through leptonema to pachynema but not to diplonema.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by histological data (Figure 1I), TUNEL assay (Figures 1J-K), and cytological evaluation (Figure 1L). The data clearly demonstrate the arrest at pachynema stage.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes display normal pachytene entry, no gross synapsis defects, and reach mid-pachynema as shown by H1t accumulation, unlike previous ATR/TOPBP1 conditional knockout models.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by SYCP1/SYCP3 staining and H1t marker data (Figure 1L), with appropriate comparison to published models. This represents a key distinction from prior work.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 MEFs show no sensitivity to hydroxyurea or phleomycin, can activate DDR signaling, recruit MDC1 to DSB foci, and show no increase in micronuclei.
evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by clonogenic survival assays (Figures 2A-D), western blots (Figure 2E), immunofluorescence (Figure 2F), and micronuclei quantification (Figure 2—supplement 2). These demonstrate normal somatic DDR function.

result: Flag-TOPBP1-B5 shows impaired binding to BLM and 53BP1, and displays twofold reduced protein levels compared to wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data (Figure 2—supplement 3). The reduced protein levels are noted with potential explanations cited from literature, though the exact mechanism remains uncertain.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes display normal DSB repair with γH2AX confined to XY chromosomes, RAD51 localized only to XY during mid-pachytene, normal HORMAD1/2 patterns, and SYCP1 overlapping SYCP3 on all autosomes.
evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 3A-E and supplements). These demonstrate normal progression through early prophase I events including synapsis and DSB repair on autosomes.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes show significantly increased MLH1 foci but no significant change in MLH3 foci.
evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 3—supplement 2). The imbalance between MLH1 and MLH3 is noted but its functional significance cannot be determined without diplotene cells to assess crossing over.

result: The sex body appears normal in shape and formation in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, with only subtle defects in γH2AX spreading at PAR and pericentromeric regions affecting 56% of mid-pachytene cells.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 3A, supplements 3-4). The subtle defect is well-characterized and quantified, though its biological significance relative to the severe phenotype is unclear.

result: TOPBP1, ATR, BRCA1, MDC1, and 53BP1 localize normally to XY chromosomes in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, and canonical ATR signaling markers (pMDC1 T4, pCHK1 S345, pHORMAD2) are mostly normal.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 3F-H, 4A-F, Figure 3—supplement 1). This demonstrates that the B5 mutation does not grossly impair DDR protein recruitment or canonical ATR signaling.

result: CHK1 S317 phosphorylation is significantly decreased in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, but this is unlikely to cause the infertility based on Chek1 CKO phenotypes.
evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by quantification (Figure 4G-H). Claim C33 is an inference based on published Chek1 CKO data (Abe et al., 2018), which is reasonable but represents interpretation rather than direct demonstration.

result: Phosphoproteomic analysis shows ATR signaling is not drastically impaired in Topbp1B5/B5 testes, but SETX phosphorylation at multiple sites including S/T-Q motifs is downregulated.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by phosphoproteomic data (Figure 5A-B) with appropriate comparison to published datasets. This identifies a specific defect in SETX regulation while confirming overall ATR signaling is intact.

result: SETX was previously associated with meiotic ATR functions and is indispensable for MSCI, and mice treated with ATR inhibitor or lacking Rad1 show reduced SETX phosphorylation and mislocalization.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by citations to published work (Becherel et al., 2013; Yeo et al., 2015; Sims et al., 2022). This establishes the context for investigating SETX in the current model.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 pachytene spermatocytes show significantly decreased SETX spreading to XY chromatin loops while maintaining SETX at unsynapsed XY axes.
evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by immunofluorescence data including 3D-SIM (Figure 5C-F). This provides a specific molecular defect that could explain the MSCI phenotype.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes form grossly normal sex bodies with normal patterns of sex body markers (CHD4, SUMO, USP7), chromatin marks (H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me3, H4K16ac, H4ac, H2AK116ub, H3K4me1), and proper RNA Pol2 exclusion.
evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by extensive immunofluorescence data (Figure 3—supplement 3, Figure 6—supplements 1-6). This demonstrates that sex body formation and most chromatin modifications are intact despite the silencing defect.

result: Single-cell RNA sequencing shows Topbp1B5/B5 germ cells contain only somatic cells, spermatogonia, and early spermatocytes, and these cells can initiate MSCI with robust but incomplete X chromosome silencing, with increased XY gene expression in the last captured spermatocyte stage.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by scRNAseq data (Figure 6D-E, supplements). This provides direct molecular evidence for the MSCI defect and confirms the arrest observed cytologically.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 testicular cells show increased expression of spermatocyte-toxic genes (Zfy1, Zfy2) and other MSCI marker genes (Kdm6a, Lamp2, Zfx, Uba1y, Rhox13, Scml2) in stage 3 spermatocytes.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by scRNAseq data (Figure 6—supplements 14-15) with appropriate comparison to published MSCI-defective mutants. This confirms the MSCI defect at the molecular level.

result: During the SP2 to SP3 transition, 74 X-linked genes in Topbp1B5/B5 versus 4 in wild-type show reduced silencing, with highly expressed genes showing more severe silencing defects.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by detailed scRNAseq analysis (Figure 7B, G, supplement 2). This quantifies the specific silencing defect and identifies a correlation with pre-leptotene expression levels.

result: The Topbp1B5/B5 mouse provides a unique model uncoupling MSCI from sex body formation, representing the first DDR mutant separating XY silencing from sex body formation and the first mutation impairing TOPBP1's meiotic silencing function without disturbing synapsis and sex body formation.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are conclusions drawn from the comprehensive experimental data presented. The uniqueness of the model is supported by comparison to all prior work showing that other DDR mutants have pleiotropic defects.

result: Topbp1 null mice are embryonic lethal, TOPBP1 depletion in cell lines causes G2/M arrest and cell death, but Topbp1B5/B5 MEFs show no proliferation or DDR defects.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by citations to published work. Claim C57 is supported by the MEF data presented. Together these establish the separation-of-function nature of the B5 allele.

result: Other mutants with XY silencing defects (Ago4 null, Dicer CKO) show sub-fertility rather than complete sterility.
evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by citations to published work (Greenlee et al., 2012; Modzelewski et al., 2012). This contextualizes the severity of the Topbp1B5/B5 phenotype.

result: The B5 mutations disrupt TOPBP1 interactions with 53BP1 and BLM, and the TOPBP1-BLM interaction contributes to protein stabilization.
evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by experimental data with citations to previous reports. Claim C60 is supported by citations (Balbo Pogliano et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2013). These establish the molecular basis for the B5 allele effects.

result: Topbp1 CKO, Rad1 CKO, and Atr CKO spermatocytes display strong synapsis defects and defective pachytene entry, whereas Setx null spermatocytes complete autosomal synapsis while displaying MSCI defects.
evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by citations to published work (ElInati et al., 2017; Widger et al., 2018) and knowledge of Setx null phenotypes. This establishes the genetic context for interpreting the Topbp1B5/B5 phenotype.

result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes do not share all defects of Setx null spermatocytes (normal γH2AX, sumoylation, ubH2A, ATR at chromatin loops), can reach MLH1-positive crossover designation stage, and progress further in pachynema than Setx null.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are based on comparison of experimental observations with published Setx phenotypes. The data support that Topbp1B5/B5 has a more limited defect than Setx null, consistent with ATR controlling specific aspects of SETX function.

result: R-loops affect chromatin architecture and interfere with transcription factor recruitment, highly transcribed genes accumulate more R-loops, and such genes show increased silencing defects in Topbp1B5/B5.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by citations to published work. Claim C68 is supported by experimental observations (Figure 7G). Together these support a model involving R-loop regulation in the MSCI defect.

result: Blm CKO mice display severe prophase I defects including incorrect pairing/synapsis and defective recombination intermediate processing leading to increased chiasmata.
evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by citation to published work (Holloway et al., 2010). This provides context for discussing potential BLM-related defects in Topbp1B5/B5.

result: MLH1 and MLH3 form a heterodimer in meiotic recombination, with MLH3 working exclusively with MLH1 while MLH1 can function with other MutL homologs.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are supported by citations to published work (Lipkin et al., 2000; Svetlanov et al., 2008; Nakagawa et al., 1999). This provides context for interpreting the MLH1/MLH3 imbalance observed.

result: Short-term (4 hr) ATR inhibitor treatment causes complete loss of γH2AX, pMDC1, and SETX from XY chromosomes, and 24 hr treatment shows complete γH2AX recovery 3 hr after release.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by citations to published work (Abe et al., 2022; Sims et al., 2022). This establishes the dynamic nature of ATR signaling and MSCI maintenance.
